summary:
NASA plans to run Moon and Mars habitats at 8.2 psia and 34% oxygen, but almost every spacecraft fire test was run near 1 atm and 21% oxygen, in microgravity. Ember Atlas is a web app that answers one question: how relevant is NASA's existing fire research to those habitats?

We compiled 1,732 burn records, 30 investigations and 54 findings from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics repository and NASA publications. Ember Atlas grades them against any habitat atmosphere. Every answer carries an evidence grade (Measured, Interpolated, Extrapolated, Analog or No data), its distance from the target condition, the NASA sources behind it and a plain "what we don't know" statement.

An envelope map, a condition matcher, ranked insights and Ask Atlas, an AI assistant limited to the NASA dataset, show where the evidence runs out. Only 3.3% of tests are near the exploration atmosphere. No solid material has burned above 31% oxygen in microgravity. Only four tests have ever left microgravity.

This matters because fire is one of the most serious risks in a sealed habitat. Designers need to know which decisions rest on real flight data and which rest on extrapolation.
details:
What it does

Ember Atlas turns scattered NASA microgravity combustion results into graded, traceable evidence for a chosen habitat atmosphere.

- Home: the challenge question, a chart placing every NASA burn against the selected habitat, a "what NASA has tested / what is missing" panel, headline numbers computed from the data, and insights ranked for that habitat.

- Check a habitat (Condition Matcher): enter any oxygen level, pressure, gravity, fuel and material. It returns an evidence grade, the five nearest real tests with their differences, relevant findings, data caveats and the experiment that would close the gap. Results are shareable links.

- Explore evidence (Envelope Map): all 1,732 tests plotted by pressure and oxygen, with habitat markers, coverage areas, oxygen partial-pressure guides and a gravity overlay.

- Ask Atlas: plain-language questions answered by Google Gemini. It can only answer through search and grading tools over the NASA dataset. Every answer cites its sources, and any citation not found in the tool results is removed. If the model is unavailable, a template-based fallback (Atlas Lite) answers from the same search.

- Library and Family Tree: every record and investigation is searchable, with quality flags in plain English and known discrepancies shown. The Family Tree keeps NASA-stated lineage (such as Saffire I→VI and LUCI→FM2) separate from links the team computed.

- Learn, Earth Applications and Fire Watch: nine short sourced lessons with quizzes, findings grouped by Earth benefit, and a three-minute habitat game where every outcome is a real NASA finding.

- Data & Method: the full pipeline, rejected rows, discrepancies, CSV/JSON downloads and the AI disclosure.

How it works

- Distance: the dataset's own distance formula measures how far each test is from the habitat atmosphere.

- Grading: the team's grading rules check whether a condition is close to a measured test, inside the tested range for the same fuel and gravity, outside it, or covered only by other conditions.

- Ranking: a transparent five-factor score ranks findings: habitat proximity, evidence strength, safety consequence, gravity match and recency. Users can adjust the weights.

Benefits and intended impact

- Habitat designers see which conditions have flight data and which tests are still missing, such as solid materials at 34% O₂ and about 55 kPa, and anything at Mars gravity.

- Reviewers can trace every number to a NASA source ID.

- Students and the public learn why fire behaves differently in space.

- Positioning: results are clearly labelled as research screening, not safety certification.

Tools

- Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4.

- Libraries: Plotly.js for charts, React Flow for the graph, MiniSearch for full-text search.

- Testing: Vitest unit tests and Playwright checks.

- AI and hosting: Google Gemini API for Ask Atlas, hosted on Vercel.

- Development assistant: Anthropic Claude (via Claude Code), disclosed in the app and in the page metadata.

- Hardware: none.

What makes it creative

- Instead of only summarizing the research, Ember Atlas grades how far each piece of evidence stretches to a new atmosphere.

- It treats "No data" as a real answer, and says what experiment would provide it.

- The game and the lessons draw on the same question bank and sources as the analysis tools.

Factors we considered

- Honesty about gaps: missing values show as "—", nominal values are marked "≈", and every grade states what is unknown.

- No AI-invented data: the assistant can only answer through tools over the dataset.

- Accessibility: WCAG AA contrast, keyboard and screen-reader support, and 44px touch targets.

- Ease of use: a first-time-user path through five core steps.

- Speed: mostly pre-rendered pages.

Source code: https://github.com/rakshithnair-netizen/emberatlas-teamneutron-spaceapps
